text: The ideal surface is z = (x² + y²)/(4f). Each ray reflects using d′ = d − 2(d·n)n and reaches (0, 0, f). Equal path lengths from the entry plane give equal arrival times at the focus.
basis: ideal-prime-focus: ideal-focus.test.ts independently checks reflected focus direction and equal optical paths; NASA Basics of Space Flight chapter 6 Reflection. Surface and on-axis incoming rays are ideal assumptions.

text: Calc. reflection uses the same vector law at each planar surface; ray intersections are solved with plane equations. For a fixed ray and a single plane of rotation, the reflected direction changes by twice the mirror angle. Incoming light follows the solved path in reverse (optical reciprocity). Assumed mirror spacing, apertures, angles, screen, trail, and playback are drawing choices. The screen shows viewing directions, not a ground footprint, detector image, or scan schedule. The feedback animation illustrates roles without a servo-response model. The public civil ABI uses scan-mirror drives and optical encoder electronics: NOAA GOES-R Data Book, Table 3-6. This diagram is not its optical layout.
basis: ideal-scan-reflection: scan-optics.test.ts plane intersections, reciprocity and double-angle checks; NASA reflection principle. ABI motor/encoder roles: NOAA GOES-R Data Book Table 3-6, printed 3-17/PDF45. All drawn spacing/angles/servo motion explicitly assumed.

text: Missile-warning satellites watch the whole Earth for the infrared heat of a rocket launch. Some sit in geostationary orbit, 35,786 km above Earth, keeping pace with the planet’s turn. Follow that heat from a rising plume, across space, through a telescope and a cold detector, and down to the ground.
basis: noaa-geo-definition definition paragraph supports 35,786 km for the circular equatorial example; gao-21-105249 printed p. 4 (PDF p. 8) describes SBIRS satellites in geosynchronous and highly elliptical orbits and is titled Missile Warning Satellites. No payload performance stated.

text: An infrared detector senses heat, so warmth inside the instrument competes with the light it is trying to measure. The detector has to run far colder than the spacecraft around it. A cooler pulls heat out of the detector, and that heat, plus the power the cooler uses, must still leave the spacecraft through radiators. Landsat 9’s civil TIRS-2 instrument gives a published example of how cold.
basis: The only numeral is part of the mission name Landsat 9; the sentence introduces the separately cited TIRS-2 temperature fact (nasa-tirs2-build) without stating a value.

text: From the high latitudesFrom geostationary orbit, a point at 60° latitude on the satellite’s own meridian sees it 22° above the horizon. At 75° latitude it is only 6° up, and the satellite reaches the horizon at 81°. A high, tilted ellipse changes that geometry: NASA says the Molniya orbit works well for observing high latitudes. The angles are geometry only, and say nothing about what a sensor can detect.

NASA Catalog of Earth Satellite Orbits (WebFetch): under Medium Earth Orbit, “the Molniya orbit works well for observing high latitudes”; caption “high inclination (63.4°) with high eccentricity (0.722)”; “Each orbit lasts 12 hours”; “spends more time at the top of its orbit farthest from the Earth”. The geometry-only disclaimer is present. Confirmed by Independent second reviewer (Claude), 10/15/2026, third pass (research/review-third-pass-2026-10-15.md).

text: Everything warm glows in the infrared. Earth’s surface, at about 288 K (15 °C), glows mostly at long wavelengths and far less in the mid-wave infrared. Heat a gas to 1,000 K and its glow climbs steeply and shifts toward shorter wavelengths.
basis: story:ground-288k (model-blackbody assumption); planck-contrast-example: 288 K − 273.15 = 14.85 °C → “about 15 °C”. The Assumed chip is present. The 288 K band radiances, 0.771 (MWIR) and 31.4 (LWIR), bear out “mostly at long wavelengths”. The Wien peak at 1,000 K is 2.9 μm, so the glow does shift shorter. The 1,000 K is hypothetical (“Heat a gas to”), and the next note labels it illustrative. Footnoted teaching assumption, checked by Independent second reviewer (Claude), 10/15/2026, third pass (research/review-third-pass-2026-10-15.md).

text: That difference is the contrast. An ideal radiator at 1,000 K outshines an ideal one at 288 K about 3,800 times in a mid-wave band (3.8 to 4.8 μm), but only about 51 times in a long-wave band (8 to 12 μm). A mid-wave view is where hot gas stands out most.
basis: story:plume-contrast: planck-contrast-example re-derived by hand: an independent midpoint integration of the Planck law with exact CODATA h, c and k (200,000 steps) gives 0.7708 (3.8–4.8 μm) and 31.39 (8–12 μm) W m⁻² sr⁻¹ at 288 K, and 2,963.1 and 1,602.8 at 1,000 K; the ratios are 3,844 and 51.05. 3,844 → “about 3,800”; 51.05 → “about 51”. The “ideal radiator” wording and the Calc. label are correct. Confirmed by Independent second reviewer (Claude), 10/15/2026, third pass (research/review-third-pass-2026-10-15.md).

text: Read it as a trend, not a plume. The 1,000 K is a round illustrative number, not a rocket-exhaust temperature, and real exhaust glows in molecular bands rather than smoothly. The units are watts per square meter per steradian: the radiance of an ideal blackbody, before any air, optics or detector. It implies nothing about what a sensor can see.
basis: illustrative-hot-gas assumption: States the illustrative-hot-gas assumption: 1,000 K is “a round illustrative number, not a rocket-exhaust temperature”. text: A satellite that stays over one point must go around once per sidereal day, T = 86,164.09 s, the time Earth takes to turn once relative to the stars. That is 23 h 56 min 4 s. Kepler’s third law, a = (μT²/4π²)^(1/3), then gives the orbit radius, 42,164 km from Earth’s center; subtracting the equatorial radius, 6,378 km, gives the altitude, 35,786 km. Circular, equatorial orbit around a spherical Earth, satellite mass neglected, perturbations omitted. NOAA gives the same altitude and NASA gives the same period, so those pages corroborate the result.
basis: geo-sidereal-kepler: geo-sidereal-kepler re-derived by hand: a = (μT²/4π²)^(1/3) = 42,164.17 km; minus 6,378.137 km = 35,786.03 km. T = 86,164.09 s = 23 h 56 min 4.09 s. The formula a = (μT²/4π²)^(1/3) is Eq. 4 with m2 neglected. The stated simplifications (circular, equatorial, spherical Earth, satellite mass neglected, no perturbations) are present. Confirmed by Independent second reviewer (Claude), 10/15/2026, third pass (research/review-third-pass-2026-10-15.md).

text: Altitude, period and one-way light time are the orbit-altitude, orbit-period and vacuum-light-time results for the same teaching orbits. Share of Earth in view is the spherical-cap fraction (1 − R/r)/2 of Earth’s surface that lies above the horizon of a point at orbital radius r from Earth’s center (R is Earth’s radius). It applies no minimum elevation angle, no field of view and no sensor, so it is geometry, not coverage, revisit or performance. HEO is evaluated at apogee, like the other HEO calculations.
basis: orbit-compare method text: The cap fraction (1 − cos θ)/2 with cos θ = R/r gives (1 − R/r)/2, which is correct. The no-elevation, no-FOV, not-coverage caveat is present, and HEO at apogee matches the table. Confirmed by Independent second reviewer (Claude), 10/15/2026, third pass (research/review-third-pass-2026-10-15.md).

text: elevation = atan2(cos ψ − R/r, sin ψ), where ψ is the central angle between a ground point and the point directly below the satellite (for a GEO satellite on the equator, the latitude on the same meridian) and r is the orbital radius. The satellite sits on the horizon where cos ψ = R/r. Spherical Earth; no terrain, no atmospheric refraction and no minimum-elevation rule. It is a geometric viewing angle and says nothing about what any sensor can or cannot detect.
basis: horizon-elevation method text: Derived: sin e = (r cos ψ − R)/d and cos e = r sin ψ/d, so tan e = (cos ψ − R/r)/sin ψ, with the horizon at cos ψ = R/r. Correct, with the no-sensor caveat. Confirmed by Independent second reviewer (Claude), 10/15/2026, third pass (research/review-third-pass-2026-10-15.md).

text: For two ideal blackbodies, one at 288 K and one at an assumed 1,000 K, integrate the Planck spectral radiance over the teaching bands 3.8–4.8 μm and 8–12 μm with the same quadrature as the band-radiance calculation, then divide the hot value by the ground value. Emissivity is 1; there is no atmosphere, no molecular band structure, no optics and no detector. Real exhaust emits in molecular bands and varies in temperature along the plume, so this shows only how contrast changes with temperature and wavelength.
basis: planck-contrast-example method text: The procedure matches the code (integratePlanckBand over both bands, hot ÷ ground) and the independent re-derivation. The caveats about molecular bands and the temperature profile are present. Confirmed by Independent second reviewer (Claude), 10/15/2026, third pass (research/review-third-pass-2026-10-15.md).
